common_name: Ann Blair Brown Camellia (Solid Pink Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this is the solid-pink parent of the variegated sport Ann Blair Brown Variegated already grown in Southern gardens.

directions: Ann Blair Brown bears large, loose, peony-form flowers in a solid, rich rose-pink, opening on a vigorous, upright, well-branched evergreen shrub during the midseason camellia bloom window. It is the un-variegated parent of the popular sport Ann Blair Brown Variegated, which carries the same peony form but with rose-pink petals marbled in white; gardeners who want the plain solid-pink flower rather than the variegated pattern grow this straight cultivar instead. Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade or filtered light, and mulch well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Prune lightly to shape immediately after flowering, since next season's buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Sun Glow Hosta (Thick-Textured Solid Gold Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a medium-large, solid gold-leaved hosta and the un-variegated parent of the widely grown sport Inniswood.

directions: Sun Glow forms a dense, medium-large mound of thick, heavily quilted, glossy gold leaves that hold their rich color from spring through fall with a little morning sun, deepening toward true gold rather than staying chartreuse in fuller shade. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in summer, though the substantial gold foliage carries most of the ornamental interest. The heavy leaf substance gives good resistance to slug damage compared with thinner-leaved gold hostas, and vigorous plants form a full clump within a few seasons. It is the un-variegated parent of the widely grown sport Inniswood, which added a dark green leaf margin to the same gold base color; grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Rainbow Gold Bearded Iris (Buttercup-Yellow Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; hybridized by Gordon Plough and registered in 1959, later used as a parent of the Tall Bearded iris Milestone.

directions: Hybridized by Gordon Plough from a cross of Butterscotch Kiss with a seedling combining Ruth, Rainbow Room, and Mary Randall, and registered in 1959, Rainbow Gold is a Tall Bearded iris carrying an intense, saturated buttercup-yellow self set off by a tangerine-orange beard. It blooms on sturdy 34-inch stems over an early-to-late season and earned an Honorable Mention in 1960 and an Award of Merit in 1962 from the American Iris Society. Rainbow Gold was later crossed with Whole Cloth to produce the popular Tall Bearded iris Milestone, making it a notable ancestor in mid-20th-century bearded iris breeding lines. Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to the sun in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Shogun Tulip (Multi-Flowered Melon and Copper Botanical Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a multi-flowered selection of the wild species Tulipa praestans, sharing that parentage with the scarlet-flowered Fusilier already in the collection.

directions: Shogun is a multi-flowered selection of the wild species Tulipa praestans, opening three to four cup-shaped blooms per stem in a warm blend of melon, pumpkin, and copper-yellow overlaid with variable red streaks and set off by bluish-black stamens. The downy, gray-green, lance-shaped leaves are fringed with fine hairs along the margin, giving the foliage a slightly fuzzy texture distinct from smooth-leaved hybrid tulips. Like the wild species and its scarlet-flowered sibling Fusilier, it is a vigorous, reliable naturalizer in lean, sharply drained soil, returning and multiplying for years rather than declining after the first season the way many large hybrid tulips do. Plant bulbs in a rock garden, gravel bed, or front-of-border drift where the clustered blooms can be appreciated at close range, and allow the foliage to yellow fully before removing it.

common_name: Heady Wine Daylily (Cream and Wine-Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; registered with the American Hemerocallis Society and used as the pollen parent of the reblooming cultivar Just Plum Happy.

directions: Registered with the American Hemerocallis Society, Heady Wine bears large, roughly five-inch cream flowers with a rich wine-purple eye zone that gives the cultivar its name, carried on well-branched scapes held above a full, grassy clump. It flowers over the midseason window typical of older diploid daylily breeding lines and was later used as the pollen parent of the reblooming introduction Just Plum Happy, passing on its distinctive cream-and-wine eye pattern. Like other daylilies it grows easily in average, well-drained soil with routine watering and tolerates summer heat well. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigorous bloom.
